catalog_quote: Stress in Maithili is far weaker than in English. Also, stress in Maithili is less significant, playing only a marginal role in distinguishing words. Below a preliminary study of the position of primary word stress in Maithili is given. ... Disyllabic: A great majority of disyllabic nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and verb infinitives receive stress on their penultimate syllable ... A number of disyllabic nouns, pronouns, and adjectives of Maithili may normally receive stress on the ultimate syllable when the ultimate syllable is either closed, i.e., ends in a consonant or a cluster of consonants, or ends in a sequence of vowels – which is diphthongized in actual pronunciation, e.g., [biˈrar] ... [ghəˈmənḍ] ... [biˈlai] ... Trisyllabic: The majority of trisyllabic nouns, pronouns, and adjectives receive stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g., [kənˈpəṭṭi] ... A small number of trisyllabic…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on pp.46-48 of Yadav 1996 in the page images we hold (leaf26/leaf27); locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1996 Mouton reference grammar by the language's principal native-speaker phonetician, whose stress section condenses his 1984 phonology monograph (Yadav 1984 ch.5, downloaded now from archive.org). Yadav 1984 confirms every clause of our 'weight-hedged, right-edge, CVC + vowel-sequence final attracts stress, default penult' reading and refines it with counts (25% of disyllabic nominals final-stressed, all heavy-final; exceptions ['bahut], ['thehun]) and with an explicit statement that vowel length is nonphonemic, so 'CVV' in what counts as heavy: must be read as diphthong/vowel sequence, which the record's 'heavy' field already says. It also documents why StressTyp2/Hayes (from S. Jha 1958's length-based rules) disagrees - Yadav rejects that premise -

sources.quote: p.107: 'Maithili, like most Indo-Aryan languages, is a stress language. However, stress in Maithili is far weaker than in English... playing only a marginal role in distinguishing words.' p.108 (on S. Jha 1958:59-60 and Grierson): 'previous writers have tended to confuse stress with vowel length... vowel length is known to be nonphonemic in Maithili. Consequently, the basic premise of these stress rules is untenable.' 5.3 (Trail 1973 list, ~1700 words): monosyllables always stressed; 'All disyllabic verbs ... and a great majority of the disyllabic nouns, pronouns and adjectives (approximately
sources.locator: Ch.5 'Acoustic analysis of word stress', printed pp.107-119 (sec.5.2 Previous studies pp.107-108; 5.3 Location of stress pp.108-112; 5.4 Acoustic correlates pp.112-119); lines 8639-9440; text-PDF leaves 116-128
sources.note: The original of the 1996 grammar's stress section: gives the percentages (disyllabic nominals 75% penult / 25% final-heavy; trisyllabic 75/18/7), the explicit rejection of vowel-length-based rules, and the only instrumental stress data; should be added to the record's sources alongside Yadav 1996.
